§1926.1400 Scope Coverage starts with power-operated equipment used in construction that can hoist, lower and horizontally move a suspended load. The list includes many crane types, derricks, dedicated pile drivers, service/mechanic trucks with a hoisting device, and variations, and it is not exhaustive [29cfr1926.1400(a)]. Multi-purpose machines are listed when configured to do this with a winch or hook [29cfr1926.1400(a)]. Attachments, whether crane-attached or suspended, don't remove covered equipment from scope [29cfr1926.1400(b)].

Check the exclusions. Machinery converted for non-hoisting use is excluded while so converted [29cfr1926.1400(c)(1)]. Excavators, backhoes, power shovels and listed loaders are excluded even when lifting with rigging [29cfr1926.1400(c)(2)]. Forklifts are excluded except when configured to hoist with a winch or hook and move a suspended load [29cfr1926.1400(c)(8)]. A mechanic's truck is excluded when used in equipment maintenance and repair activities [29cfr1926.1400(c)(9)]. Wreckers, digger derricks, aerial devices, tree work and other listed items also have exclusions, some conditional [29cfr1926.1400(c)]. Digger derrick work under subpart V or telecommunication construction must meet stated compliance conditions to qualify [29cfr1926.1400(c)(4)].

For articulating/knuckle-boom delivery cranes, ground transfer is excluded when materials aren't arranged in a particular sequence for hoisting [29cfr1926.1400(c)(17)(i)]. Placing building supply sheet goods or packaged materials onto a structure is excluded when using a boom-end fork/cradle, "but only when the truck crane is equipped with a properly functioning automatic overload prevention device" [29cfr1926.1400(c)(17)(ii)]. The exclusion doesn't apply when holding, supporting or stabilizing material to facilitate construction [29cfr1926.1400(c)(17)(iii)(A)], or when handling prefabricated components [29cfr1926.1400(c)(17)(iii)(B)] or structural steel members or systems-engineered metal building components [29cfr1926.1400(c)(17)(iii)(C)].

Employers must establish, effectively communicate and enforce work rules ensuring compliance with provisions directing employee actions [29cfr1926.1400(f)]. Controlling entity duties include those in the sections named in [29cfr1926.1400(e)]. “Such attachments, whether crane-attached or suspended include, but are not limited to: Hooks, magnets, grapples, clamshell buckets, orange peel buckets, concrete buckets, drag lines, personnel platforms, augers or drills and pile driving equipment. (c) Exclusions. This subpart does not cover: (1) Machinery included in paragraph (a) of this section while it has been converted or adapted for a non-hoisting/lifting use. Such conversions/adaptations include, but are not limited to, power shovels, excavators and concrete pumps.”

For articulating/knuckle-boom delivery cranes, ground transfer is excluded when materials aren't arranged in a particular sequence for hoisting [29cfr1926.1400(c)(17)(i)]. Placing building supply sheet goods or packaged materials onto a structure is excluded when using a boom-end fork/cradle, "but only when the truck crane is equipped with a properly functioning automatic overload prevention device" [29cfr1926.1400(c)(17)(ii)]. The exclusion doesn't apply when holding, supporting or stabilizing material to facilitate construction [29cfr1926.1400(c)(17)(iii)(A)], or when handling prefabricated components [29cfr1926.1400(c)(17)(iii)(B)] or structural steel members or systems-engineered metal building components [29cfr1926.1400(c)(17)(iii)(C)].

Employers must establish, effectively communicate and enforce work rules ensuring compliance with provisions directing employee actions [29cfr1926.1400(f)]. Controlling entity duties include those in the sections named in [29cfr1926.1400(e)]. “(5) Machinery originally designed as vehicle-mounted aerial devices (for lifting personnel) and self-propelled elevating work platforms. (6) Telescopic/hydraulic gantry systems. (7) Stacker cranes. (8) Powered industrial trucks (forklifts), except when configured to hoist and lower (by means of a winch or hook) and horizontally move a suspended load.” §1926.1401 Definitions These definitions control how the subpart's terms are read [29cfr1926.1401]. "Include/including" and "Such as" introduce non-exhaustive examples, and "Up to" means "up to and including." Load covers the hoisted objects and load-attaching equipment, such as the load block, ropes and slings, whether the term refers to the objects or their weight. Rated capacity is the manufacturer's maximum working load under specified conditions, typically involving configuration, radius and boom length [29cfr1926.1401].

Know your devices. A load moment (rated capacity) indicator compares the lifting condition with rated capacity and shows the percentage in use. A limiter, once rated capacity is reached, cuts power to functions that can increase loading severity; functions that reduce it typically remain operational. A boom hoist limiting device disengages boom hoist power at a predetermined angle and prevents lowering afterward by setting brakes or closing valves. Range control devices are operator-set: one limits boom or jib tip movement, the other warns. Operational aids provide information or automatically take control of a function, including those listed in § 1926.1416 [29cfr1926.1401].

For lowering, controlled load lowering uses the hoist drive motor rather than the load hoist brake. In free fall, only the brake regulates descent [29cfr1926.1401].

Near power lines, a dedicated spotter must meet § 1926.1428 and has the sole responsibility of watching separation and communicating with you so the minimum approach distance is not breached. A dedicated channel is assigned to "only one signal person and crane/derrick" or to a coordinated group. The employer controlling the communication system assigns it [29cfr1926.1401].

The fall zone extends beyond the area directly under the load to wherever suspended materials could foreseeably fall in an accident. Assembly/disassembly terms change for tower cranes to "erecting and climbing" and "dismantling." Any height increase is erection. Dismantling includes partial dismantling [29cfr1926.1401].

A multi-purpose machine is covered when configured with a winch pack, a jib with a hook, or a jib used with a winch, but not when configured with forks or tongs [29cfr1926.1401]. “Moving point-to-point means the times during which an employee is in the process of going to or from a work station. Multi-purpose machine means a machine that is designed to be configured in various ways, at least one of which allows it to hoist (by means of a winch or hook) and horizontally move a suspended load. For example, a machine that can rotate and can be configured with removable forks/tongs (for use as a forklift) or with a winch pack, jib (with a hook at the end) or jib used in conjunction with a winch.”

§1926.1401 Definitions These definitions control how the subpart's terms are read [29cfr1926.1401]. "Include/including" and "Such as" introduce non-exhaustive examples, and "Up to" means "up to and including." Load covers the hoisted objects and load-attaching equipment, such as the load block, ropes and slings, whether the term refers to the objects or their weight. Rated capacity is the manufacturer's maximum working load under specified conditions, typically involving configuration, radius and boom length [29cfr1926.1401].

Know your devices. A load moment (rated capacity) indicator compares the lifting condition with rated capacity and shows the percentage in use. A limiter, once rated capacity is reached, cuts power to functions that can increase loading severity; functions that reduce it typically remain operational. A boom hoist limiting device disengages boom hoist power at a predetermined angle and prevents lowering afterward by setting brakes or closing valves. Range control devices are operator-set: one limits boom or jib tip movement, the other warns. Operational aids provide information or automatically take control of a function, including those listed in § 1926.1416 [29cfr1926.1401].

For lowering, controlled load lowering uses the hoist drive motor rather than the load hoist brake. In free fall, only the brake regulates descent [29cfr1926.1401].

Near power lines, a dedicated spotter must meet § 1926.1428 and has the sole responsibility of watching separation and communicating with you so the minimum approach distance is not breached. A dedicated channel is assigned to "only one signal person and crane/derrick" or to a coordinated group. The employer controlling the communication system assigns it [29cfr1926.1401].

The fall zone extends beyond the area directly under the load to wherever suspended materials could foreseeably fall in an accident. Assembly/disassembly terms change for tower cranes to "erecting and climbing" and "dismantling." Any height increase is erection. Dismantling includes partial dismantling [29cfr1926.1401].

A multi-purpose machine is covered when configured with a winch pack, a jib with a hook, or a jib used with a winch, but not when configured with forks or tongs [29cfr1926.1401]. “Dismantling includes partial dismantling (such as dismantling to shorten a boom or substitute a different component). Drum rotation indicator means a device on a crane or hoist which indicates in which direction and at what relative speed a particular hoist drum is turning. Electrical contact occurs when a person, object, or equipment makes contact or comes in close proximity with an energized conductor or equipment that allows the passage of current. Employer-made equipment means floating cranes/derricks designed and built by an employer for the employer's own use.” §1926.1437 Floating cranes/derricks and land cranes/derricks on barges This supplements the subpart for floating and barge-mounted cranes and derricks, excluding jacked barges fully supported by deployed jacks [29cfr1926.1437(a)]. Work area control applies except § 1926.1424(a)(2)(ii); use barriers, or signs plus equipment markings and employee training [29cfr1926.1437(c)]. § 1926.1425 doesn't apply [29cfr1926.1437(d)]. Add list/trim and house-lock devices, plus a wind indicator when a competent person finds wind relevant [29cfr1926.1437(e)]. Anti two-block applies only to personnel hoisting or hoisting over occupied cofferdams or shafts; listed work has load-weighing relief [29cfr1926.1437(f)]. Cab or no-cab information-access rules apply [29cfr1926.1437(g)].

Competent persons inspect the flotation each shift and monthly [29cfr1926.1437(h)(3)]. Annual external and four-year internal inspections require specified expertise; hazards remove the vessel from service, and flagged nonhazards are monitored [29cfr1926.1437(h)(4)] [29cfr1926.1437(h)(5)]. Document monthly, annual and four-year inspections; keep four-year records at least 4 years [29cfr1926.1437(h)(6)].

Diver work requires dedicated crane use until all divers return, continuous control attendance, tender sightline or electronic signals, and no-shift securing [29cfr1926.1437(j)]. Don't exceed vessel environmental, operating or transit limits [29cfr1926.1437(k)].

For permanent marine equipment, follow water charts and their parameters; charts consider minimum 40 mph wind [29cfr1926.1437(m)(1)]. List/trim maximums, in degrees, are 5 each at 25 tons or less, 7 over 25, and 10 for derricks [29cfr1926.1437-table-M1]. Stability: 60 mph with 2 ft freeboard at rated capacity or high boom/no load; 1 ft at capacity plus 25% [29cfr1926.1437-table-M2]; backward stability, high boom/no load/full back list, 90 mph [29cfr1926.1437-table-M3]. Employer-made equipment needs engineer-signed proof [29cfr1926.1437(m)(4)].

Land equipment needs expert derating [29cfr1926.1437(n)(2)]. Vessel list/trim cannot exceed the least of 5 degrees or the manufacturer's limit (qualified person's if unspecified), and must preserve above-water decks and a fully submerged bottom [29cfr1926.1437(n)(3)(i)] [29cfr1926.1437(n)(4)]. Crane list/trim limits also apply [29cfr1926.1437(n)(3)(ii)]. Secure by attachment, corral, rails or centerline cable, except qualifying mobile auxiliaries under a plan [29cfr1926.1437(n)]. Both equipment categories have hull requirements [29cfr1926.1437(m)(5)] [29cfr1926.1437(n)(7)]. “The requirements of this section do not apply when using jacked barges when the jacks are deployed to the river, lake, or sea bed and the barge is fully supported by the jacks. (b) General requirements. The requirements in paragraphs (c) through (k) of this section apply to both floating cranes/derricks and land cranes/derricks on barges, pontoons, vessels or other means of flotation. (c) Work area control. (1) The requirements of § 1926.1424 (Work area control) apply, except for § 1926.1424(a)(2)(ii).”

§1926.1402(f) “(f) This section does not apply to cranes designed for use on railroad tracks when used on railroad tracks that are part of the general railroad system of transportation that is regulated pursuant to the Federal Railroad Administration under 49 CFR part 213 and that comply with applicable Federal Railroad Administration requirements.” §1926.1402 Ground conditions Do not assemble or use the equipment unless the ground is firm, drained and graded enough to meet the manufacturer's specifications for adequate support and degree of level. You may count supporting materials, if necessary, toward meeting them. Drainage is not required in marshes or wetlands [29cfr1926.1402(b)]. Ground conditions include slope, compaction and firmness [29cfr1926.1402(a)(1)]. Supporting materials include blocking, mats, cribbing, marsh buggies in marshes or wetlands, and similar materials or devices [29cfr1926.1402(a)(2)].

The controlling entity must ensure the necessary ground preparations are provided [29cfr1926.1402(c)(1)]. It must also inform the equipment user and operator of the location of hazards beneath the set-up area, such as voids, tanks and utilities. This paragraph does not apply to the inspection of ground conditions for railroad tracks and their underlying support when the railroad tracks are part of the general railroad system of transportation that is regulated pursuant to the Federal Railroad Administration under 49 CFR part 213.” §1926.1401 Definitions These definitions control how the subpart's terms are read [29cfr1926.1401]. "Include/including" and "Such as" introduce non-exhaustive examples, and "Up to" means "up to and including." Load covers the hoisted objects and load-attaching equipment, such as the load block, ropes and slings, whether the term refers to the objects or their weight. Rated capacity is the manufacturer's maximum working load under specified conditions, typically involving configuration, radius and boom length [29cfr1926.1401].

Know your devices. A load moment (rated capacity) indicator compares the lifting condition with rated capacity and shows the percentage in use. A limiter, once rated capacity is reached, cuts power to functions that can increase loading severity; functions that reduce it typically remain operational. A boom hoist limiting device disengages boom hoist power at a predetermined angle and prevents lowering afterward by setting brakes or closing valves. Range control devices are operator-set: one limits boom or jib tip movement, the other warns. Operational aids provide information or automatically take control of a function, including those listed in § 1926.1416 [29cfr1926.1401].

For lowering, controlled load lowering uses the hoist drive motor rather than the load hoist brake. In free fall, only the brake regulates descent [29cfr1926.1401].

Near power lines, a dedicated spotter must meet § 1926.1428 and has the sole responsibility of watching separation and communicating with you so the minimum approach distance is not breached. A dedicated channel is assigned to "only one signal person and crane/derrick" or to a coordinated group. The employer controlling the communication system assigns it [29cfr1926.1401].

The fall zone extends beyond the area directly under the load to wherever suspended materials could foreseeably fall in an accident. Assembly/disassembly terms change for tower cranes to "erecting and climbing" and "dismantling." Any height increase is erection. Dismantling includes partial dismantling [29cfr1926.1401].

A multi-purpose machine is covered when configured with a winch pack, a jib with a hook, or a jib used with a winch, but not when configured with forks or tongs [29cfr1926.1401]. “It compares this lifting condition to the equipment's rated capacity, and when the rated capacity is reached, it shuts off power to those equipment functions which can increase the severity of loading on the equipment, e.g., hoisting, telescoping out, or luffing out. Typically, those functions which decrease the severity of loading on the equipment remain operational, e.g., lowering, telescoping in, or luffing in. Locomotive crane means a crane mounted on a base or car equipped for travel on a railroad track.”

§1926.1401 Definitions These definitions control how the subpart's terms are read [29cfr1926.1401]. "Include/including" and "Such as" introduce non-exhaustive examples, and "Up to" means "up to and including." Load covers the hoisted objects and load-attaching equipment, such as the load block, ropes and slings, whether the term refers to the objects or their weight. Rated capacity is the manufacturer's maximum working load under specified conditions, typically involving configuration, radius and boom length [29cfr1926.1401].

Know your devices. A load moment (rated capacity) indicator compares the lifting condition with rated capacity and shows the percentage in use. A limiter, once rated capacity is reached, cuts power to functions that can increase loading severity; functions that reduce it typically remain operational. A boom hoist limiting device disengages boom hoist power at a predetermined angle and prevents lowering afterward by setting brakes or closing valves. Range control devices are operator-set: one limits boom or jib tip movement, the other warns. Operational aids provide information or automatically take control of a function, including those listed in § 1926.1416 [29cfr1926.1401].

For lowering, controlled load lowering uses the hoist drive motor rather than the load hoist brake. In free fall, only the brake regulates descent [29cfr1926.1401].

Near power lines, a dedicated spotter must meet § 1926.1428 and has the sole responsibility of watching separation and communicating with you so the minimum approach distance is not breached. A dedicated channel is assigned to "only one signal person and crane/derrick" or to a coordinated group. The employer controlling the communication system assigns it [29cfr1926.1401].

The fall zone extends beyond the area directly under the load to wherever suspended materials could foreseeably fall in an accident. Assembly/disassembly terms change for tower cranes to "erecting and climbing" and "dismantling." Any height increase is erection. Dismantling includes partial dismantling [29cfr1926.1401].

A multi-purpose machine is covered when configured with a winch pack, a jib with a hook, or a jib used with a winch, but not when configured with forks or tongs [29cfr1926.1401]. “§ 1926.1401 Definitions. A/D director (Assembly/Disassembly director) means an individual who meets this subpart's requirements for an A/D director, irrespective of the person's formal job title or whether the person is non-management or management personnel. Articulating crane means a crane whose boom consists of a series of folding, pin connected structural members, typically manipulated to extend or retract by power from hydraulic cylinders.” §1926.1404 Assembly/Disassembly—general requirements (applies to all assembly and disassembly operations) Assembly/disassembly is directed by the A/D director: a competent and qualified person, or a competent person assisted by qualified persons. A lone worker must be both [29cfr1926.1404(a)]. The director must understand the procedures [29cfr1926.1404(b)], reviewing them immediately beforehand unless already understanding and having applied them to the same equipment type and configuration [29cfr1926.1404(c)]. Crew must understand tasks, hazards and locations to avoid before work, task changes or additions of personnel [29cfr1926.1404(d)].

Crew must notify you before entering covered out-of-view locations where equipment or load movement could injure them [29cfr1926.1404(e)(1)]. If you know someone went there, move no part or load until the pre-arranged communication system confirms they are safe [29cfr1926.1404(e)(2)]. Nobody may be under components during pin removal unless the employer demonstrates site constraints require it; the director must then minimize movement risk and exposure [29cfr1926.1404(f)].

Rated capacity limits apply in all phases [29cfr1926.1404(g)]. The director addresses ground, blocking, assist crane loads (verified beforehand), pick points, center of gravity, stability at pin removal, snagging, counterweights, backward stability and weather [29cfr1926.1404(h)]. Test the boom hoist brake each time before relying on it; if insufficient, use another specified protection against boom movement [29cfr1926.1404(h)(10)].

Observe manufacturer cantilever limits, or if unavailable, a registered professional engineer's written limit [29cfr1926.1404(j)]. Keep component weights readily available [29cfr1926.1404(k)]. Components and configuration affecting capacity or safety follow manufacturer requirements (or written engineer approval if unavailable) or qualifying approved modifications; inspect after assembly [29cfr1926.1404(m)]. Remove and safely stow reusable shipping hardware [29cfr1926.1404(o)]. No jib during pile driving [29cfr1926.1404(p)].

Whenever outriggers or stabilizers are required or used, rules cover extension, floats, visibility and blocking; outriggers, except on locomotive cranes, must take equipment weight off wheels. Locomotive cranes have manufacturer-procedure rules [29cfr1926.1404(q)]. Rigging requires a qualified rigger, synthetic sling protection and compliance with sling manufacturer instructions and recommendations, alongside other applicable rigging standards [29cfr1926.1404(r)]. “For purposes of this standard, that person is considered the A/D director. (b) Knowledge of procedures. The A/D director must understand the applicable assembly/disassembly procedures. (c) Review of procedures. The A/D director must review the applicable assembly/disassembly procedures immediately prior to the commencement of assembly/disassembly unless the A/D director understands the procedures and has applied them to the same type and configuration of equipment (including accessories, if any).”

body.text: §1926.1404(h)(10) Boom hoist brake failure

(10) Boom hoist brake failure. Each time reliance is to be placed on the boom hoist brake to prevent boom movement during assembly/disassembly, the brake must be tested prior to such reliance to determine if it is sufficient to prevent boom movement. If it is not sufficient, a boom hoist pawl, other locking device/back-up braking device, or another method of preventing dangerous movement of the boom (such as blocking or using an assist crane) from a boom hoist brake failure must be used.

(i) On friction equipment, whenever moving a boom off a support, first raise the boom a short distance (sufficient to take the load of the boom) to determine if the boom hoist brake needs to be adjusted. On other types of equipment with a boom, the same practice is applicable, except that typically there is no means of adjusting the brake; if the brake does not hold, a repair is necessary. See § 1926.1417(f) and (j) for additional requirements.
(2) Hydraulic drums must have an integrally mounted holding device or internal static brake to prevent boom hoist movement in the event of hydraulic failure.

§1926.1401 Definitions These definitions control how the subpart's terms are read [29cfr1926.1401]. "Include/including" and "Such as" introduce non-exhaustive examples, and "Up to" means "up to and including." Load covers the hoisted objects and load-attaching equipment, such as the load block, ropes and slings, whether the term refers to the objects or their weight. Rated capacity is the manufacturer's maximum working load under specified conditions, typically involving configuration, radius and boom length [29cfr1926.1401].

Know your devices. A load moment (rated capacity) indicator compares the lifting condition with rated capacity and shows the percentage in use. A limiter, once rated capacity is reached, cuts power to functions that can increase loading severity; functions that reduce it typically remain operational. A boom hoist limiting device disengages boom hoist power at a predetermined angle and prevents lowering afterward by setting brakes or closing valves. Range control devices are operator-set: one limits boom or jib tip movement, the other warns. Operational aids provide information or automatically take control of a function, including those listed in § 1926.1416 [29cfr1926.1401].

For lowering, controlled load lowering uses the hoist drive motor rather than the load hoist brake. In free fall, only the brake regulates descent [29cfr1926.1401].

Near power lines, a dedicated spotter must meet § 1926.1428 and has the sole responsibility of watching separation and communicating with you so the minimum approach distance is not breached. A dedicated channel is assigned to "only one signal person and crane/derrick" or to a coordinated group. The employer controlling the communication system assigns it [29cfr1926.1401].

The fall zone extends beyond the area directly under the load to wherever suspended materials could foreseeably fall in an accident. Assembly/disassembly terms change for tower cranes to "erecting and climbing" and "dismantling." Any height increase is erection. Dismantling includes partial dismantling [29cfr1926.1401].

A multi-purpose machine is covered when configured with a winch pack, a jib with a hook, or a jib used with a winch, but not when configured with forks or tongs [29cfr1926.1401]. “Assist crane means a crane used to assist in assembling or disassembling a crane. Attachments means any device that expands the range of tasks that can be done by the equipment. Examples include, but are not limited to: An auger, drill, magnet, pile-driver, and boom-attached personnel platform. Audible signal means a signal made by a distinct sound or series of sounds. Examples include, but are not limited to, sounds made by a bell, horn, or whistle. Blocking (also referred to as “cribbing”) is wood or other material used to support equipment or a component and distribute loads to the ground.”

§1926.1403 Assembly/Disassembly—selection of manufacturer or employer procedures For assembly or disassembly of equipment or attachments, the employer has a fixed duty and a choice. The fixed duty is to comply with all applicable manufacturer prohibitions [29cfr1926.1403]. The choice is which procedures to comply with. The employer must use either the manufacturer procedures or its own [29cfr1926.1403].

The first option is the "Manufacturer procedures applicable to assembly and disassembly" [29cfr1926.1403(a)]. The second is employer procedures for assembly and disassembly [29cfr1926.1403(b)]. That second option is conditional: employer procedures may be used "only where the employer can demonstrate" that the procedures used meet the requirements in § 1926.1406 [29cfr1926.1403(b)]. In deciding between the two, keep in mind that the prohibitions duty is stated separately from the choice of procedures, so selecting employer procedures leaves applicable manufacturer prohibitions in force [29cfr1926.1403].

Synthetic slings affect this decision. According to the note, when an employer uses synthetic slings during assembly or disassembly rigging, the employer must follow manufacturer procedures [29cfr1926.1403-note-1]. The note refers to § 1926.1404(r) [29cfr1926.1403-note-1]. This section does not set out the contents of either § 1926.1406 or § 1926.1404(r). “§ 1926.1403 Assembly/Disassembly—selection of manufacturer or employer procedures. When assembling or disassembling equipment (or attachments), the employer must comply with all applicable manufacturer prohibitions and must comply with either: (a) Manufacturer procedures applicable to assembly and disassembly, or (b) Employer procedures for assembly and disassembly. Employer procedures may be used only where the employer can demonstrate that the procedures used meet the requirements in § 1926.1406.” §1926.1406 Assembly/Disassembly—employer procedures—general requirements When assembly or disassembly is done under employer procedures instead of manufacturer procedures, the employer has a duty to ensure those procedures meet the conditions in this section [29cfr1926.1406(a)].

The procedures must prevent two things for any part of the equipment: unintended dangerous movement and collapse [29cfr1926.1406(a)(1)]. They must also "Provide adequate support and stability of all parts of the equipment." [29cfr1926.1406(a)(2)] Note the scope of the wording: the first condition reaches "any part of the equipment" [29cfr1926.1406(a)(1)], and the support and stability condition reaches all parts [29cfr1926.1406(a)(2)].

The procedures must also address employee position. Employees involved in the assembly/disassembly operation must be positioned so that their exposure to unintended movement or collapse is minimized. This covers movement or collapse of "part or all of the equipment" [29cfr1926.1406(a)(3)]. The wording for this condition is that exposure is "minimized" [29cfr1926.1406(a)(3)].

Development of the procedures is assigned to a particular role: "Employer procedures must be developed by a qualified person." [29cfr1926.1406(b)] The text of this section gives no definition of a qualified person. It also states no numeric limits for support, stability, or employee position. “§ 1926.1406 Assembly/Disassembly—employer procedures—general requirements. (a) When using employer procedures instead of manufacturer procedures for assembly/disassembly, the employer must ensure that the procedures:”

response.text:
§1926.1404(o) Shipping pins “(o) Shipping pins. Reusable shipping pins, straps, links, and similar equipment must be removed. Once they are removed they must either be stowed or otherwise stored so that they do not present a falling object hazard.” §1926.1405 Disassembly—additional requirements for dismantling of booms and jibs (applies to both the use of manufacturer procedures and employer procedures) These additional disassembly requirements cover dismantling booms and jibs, including dismantling to change their length. They apply under both manufacturer procedures and employer procedures [29cfr1926.1405]. Each restriction covers removing a pin "partly or completely", so before moving any pin, the questions are where it is and how the boom is held.

With the pendants in tension, no pins in the pendants may be removed [29cfr1926.1405(a)]. In that same condition, no top or bottom pins may be removed on boom sections located between the pendant attachment points and the crane or derrick body [29cfr1926.1405(b)].

When the boom is supported by its uppermost section resting on the ground or other support, the restriction covers top and bottom pins on sections between that uppermost section and the crane or derrick body [29cfr1926.1405(c)].

For the cantilevered portion of the boom being removed, meaning the portion ahead of the pendant attachment points, no top pins on its boom sections may be removed "until the cantilevered section to be removed is fully supported" [29cfr1926.1405(d)]. "Include/including" and "Such as" introduce non-exhaustive examples, and "Up to" means "up to and including." Load covers the hoisted objects and load-attaching equipment, such as the load block, ropes and slings, whether the term refers to the objects or their weight. Rated capacity is the manufacturer's maximum working load under specified conditions, typically involving configuration, radius and boom length [29cfr1926.1401].

Know your devices. A load moment (rated capacity) indicator compares the lifting condition with rated capacity and shows the percentage in use. A limiter, once rated capacity is reached, cuts power to functions that can increase loading severity; functions that reduce it typically remain operational. A boom hoist limiting device disengages boom hoist power at a predetermined angle and prevents lowering afterward by setting brakes or closing valves. Range control devices are operator-set: one limits boom or jib tip movement, the other warns. Operational aids provide information or automatically take control of a function, including those listed in § 1926.1416 [29cfr1926.1401].

For lowering, controlled load lowering uses the hoist drive motor rather than the load hoist brake. In free fall, only the brake regulates descent [29cfr1926.1401].

Near power lines, a dedicated spotter must meet § 1926.1428 and has the sole responsibility of watching separation and communicating with you so the minimum approach distance is not breached. A dedicated channel is assigned to "only one signal person and crane/derrick" or to a coordinated group. The employer controlling the communication system assigns it [29cfr1926.1401].

The fall zone extends beyond the area directly under the load to wherever suspended materials could foreseeably fall in an accident. Assembly/disassembly terms change for tower cranes to "erecting and climbing" and "dismantling." Any height increase is erection. Dismantling includes partial dismantling [29cfr1926.1401].

A multi-purpose machine is covered when configured with a winch pack, a jib with a hook, or a jib used with a winch, but not when configured with forks or tongs [29cfr1926.1401]. “Examples include, but are not limited to: An auger, drill, magnet, pile-driver, and boom-attached personnel platform. Audible signal means a signal made by a distinct sound or series of sounds. Examples include, but are not limited to, sounds made by a bell, horn, or whistle. Blocking (also referred to as “cribbing”) is wood or other material used to support equipment or a component and distribute loads to the ground. It is typically used to support lattice boom sections during assembly/disassembly and under outrigger and stabilizer floats.”

The fixed duty is to comply with all applicable manufacturer prohibitions [29cfr1926.1403]. The choice is which procedures to comply with. The employer must use either the manufacturer procedures or its own [29cfr1926.1403].

The first option is the "Manufacturer procedures applicable to assembly and disassembly" [29cfr1926.1403(a)]. The second is employer procedures for assembly and disassembly [29cfr1926.1403(b)]. That second option is conditional: employer procedures may be used "only where the employer can demonstrate" that the procedures used meet the requirements in § 1926.1406 [29cfr1926.1403(b)]. In deciding between the two, keep in mind that the prohibitions duty is stated separately from the choice of procedures, so selecting employer procedures leaves applicable manufacturer prohibitions in force [29cfr1926.1403].

§1926.1408 Power line safety (up to 350 kV)—equipment operations Before operating, the employer must identify the work zone: demarcated boundaries you are prohibited from passing, or 360 degrees out to maximum working radius [29cfr1926.1408(a)(1)]. If equipment, load line or load (with rigging and accessories) could get within 20 feet of a line at that radius, one option applies: utility-confirmed deenergizing with visible worksite grounding, 20-foot clearance, or Table A clearance [29cfr1926.1408(a)(2)]. Table A (AC, nominal kV): up to 50, 10 feet; over 50 to 200, 15; over 200 to 350, 20; over 350 to 500, 25; over 500 to 750, 35; over 750 to 1,000, 45; over 1,000, set by the utility or a qualified registered professional engineer. Upper values are inclusive [29cfr1926.1408-table-A]. Requested voltage information is due from the utility within two working days [29cfr1926.1408(c)].

Where encroachment precautions are required, there must be a planning meeting, non-conductive tag lines if used, and a flagged or high-visibility warning line, barricade or sign line in your view at the applicable distance [29cfr1926.1408(b)]. At least one measure is also required: proximity alarm, dedicated spotter, automatic warning device, automatic range limiter, or insulating link/device; subpart V work is excepted from this [29cfr1926.1408(b)(4)] [29cfr1926.1408(b)(5)]. If you cannot see the warning line, a dedicated spotter is required plus one of the other four [29cfr1926.1408(b)(3)]. Spotters need continuous contact, a visual aid, effective positioning, direct communication equipment where necessary, and must give timely information [29cfr1926.1408(b)(4)(ii)].

Operating below lines requires confirmed deenergizing and worksite grounding unless an exception applies [29cfr1926.1408(d)]. Presume lines energized [29cfr1926.1408(e)]. Near transmitter towers where charge could be induced, deenergize the transmitter, or ground the equipment and use only non-conductive tag lines if any [29cfr1926.1408(f)]. Training covers contact procedures, line presumptions, device limitations and grounding [29cfr1926.1408(g)(1)]. Safety devices, aids and contact-prevention means used for compliance must meet manufacturer procedures and conditions [29cfr1926.1408(h)]. “§ 1926.1408 Power line safety (up to 350 kV)—equipment operations.”

§1926.1401 Definitions These definitions control how the subpart's terms are read [29cfr1926.1401]. "Include/including" and "Such as" introduce non-exhaustive examples, and "Up to" means "up to and including." Load covers the hoisted objects and load-attaching equipment, such as the load block, ropes and slings, whether the term refers to the objects or their weight. Rated capacity is the manufacturer's maximum working load under specified conditions, typically involving configuration, radius and boom length [29cfr1926.1401].

Know your devices. A load moment (rated capacity) indicator compares the lifting condition with rated capacity and shows the percentage in use. A limiter, once rated capacity is reached, cuts power to functions that can increase loading severity; functions that reduce it typically remain operational. A boom hoist limiting device disengages boom hoist power at a predetermined angle and prevents lowering afterward by setting brakes or closing valves. Range control devices are operator-set: one limits boom or jib tip movement, the other warns. Operational aids provide information or automatically take control of a function, including those listed in § 1926.1416 [29cfr1926.1401].

For lowering, controlled load lowering uses the hoist drive motor rather than the load hoist brake. In free fall, only the brake regulates descent [29cfr1926.1401].

Near power lines, a dedicated spotter must meet § 1926.1428 and has the sole responsibility of watching separation and communicating with you so the minimum approach distance is not breached. A dedicated channel is assigned to "only one signal person and crane/derrick" or to a coordinated group. The employer controlling the communication system assigns it [29cfr1926.1401].

The fall zone extends beyond the area directly under the load to wherever suspended materials could foreseeably fall in an accident. Assembly/disassembly terms change for tower cranes to "erecting and climbing" and "dismantling." Any height increase is erection. Dismantling includes partial dismantling [29cfr1926.1401].

A multi-purpose machine is covered when configured with a winch pack, a jib with a hook, or a jib used with a winch, but not when configured with forks or tongs [29cfr1926.1401]. “Operator means a person who is operating the equipment. Overhead and gantry cranes includes overhead/bridge cranes, semigantry, cantilever gantry, wall cranes, storage bridge cranes, launching gantry cranes, and similar equipment, irrespective of whether it travels on tracks, wheels, or other means. Paragraph refers to a paragraph in the same section of this subpart that the word “paragraph” is used, unless otherwise specified. Pendants includes both wire and bar types. Wire type: A fixed length of wire rope with mechanical fittings at both ends for pinning segments of wire rope together.”

Table A to §1926.1408 Table A—Minimum Clearance Distances “Table A—Minimum Clearance Distances Voltage (nominal, kV, alternating current) | Minimum clearance distance (feet) up to 50 | 10 over 50 to 200 | 15 over 200 to 350 | 20 over 350 to 500 | 25 over 500 to 750 | 35 over 750 to 1,000 | 45 over 1,000 | (as established by the utility owner/operator or registered professional engineer who is a qualified person with respect to electrical power transmission and distribution). Note: The value that follows “to” is up to and includes that value. For example, over 50 to 200 means up to and including 200kV.” §1926.1408 Power line safety (up to 350 kV)—equipment operations Before operating, the employer must identify the work zone: demarcated boundaries you are prohibited from passing, or 360 degrees out to maximum working radius [29cfr1926.1408(a)(1)]. If equipment, load line or load (with rigging and accessories) could get within 20 feet of a line at that radius, one option applies: utility-confirmed deenergizing with visible worksite grounding, 20-foot clearance, or Table A clearance [29cfr1926.1408(a)(2)]. Table A (AC, nominal kV): up to 50, 10 feet; over 50 to 200, 15; over 200 to 350, 20; over 350 to 500, 25; over 500 to 750, 35; over 750 to 1,000, 45; over 1,000, set by the utility or a qualified registered professional engineer. Upper values are inclusive [29cfr1926.1408-table-A]. Requested voltage information is due from the utility within two working days [29cfr1926.1408(c)].

Where encroachment precautions are required, there must be a planning meeting, non-conductive tag lines if used, and a flagged or high-visibility warning line, barricade or sign line in your view at the applicable distance [29cfr1926.1408(b)]. At least one measure is also required: proximity alarm, dedicated spotter, automatic warning device, automatic range limiter, or insulating link/device; subpart V work is excepted from this [29cfr1926.1408(b)(4)] [29cfr1926.1408(b)(5)]. If you cannot see the warning line, a dedicated spotter is required plus one of the other four [29cfr1926.1408(b)(3)]. Spotters need continuous contact, a visual aid, effective positioning, direct communication equipment where necessary, and must give timely information [29cfr1926.1408(b)(4)(ii)].

Operating below lines requires confirmed deenergizing and worksite grounding unless an exception applies [29cfr1926.1408(d)]. Presume lines energized [29cfr1926.1408(e)]. Near transmitter towers where charge could be induced, deenergize the transmitter, or ground the equipment and use only non-conductive tag lines if any [29cfr1926.1408(f)]. Training covers contact procedures, line presumptions, device limitations and grounding [29cfr1926.1408(g)(1)]. Safety devices, aids and contact-prevention means used for compliance must meet manufacturer procedures and conditions [29cfr1926.1408(h)]. “(i) Option (1)—Deenergize and ground. Confirm from the utility owner/operator that the power line has been deenergized and visibly grounded at the worksite. (ii) Option (2)—20 foot clearance. Ensure that no part of the equipment, load line, or load (including rigging and lifting accessories), gets closer than 20 feet to the power line by implementing the measures specified in paragraph (b) of this section. (iii) Option (3)—Table A clearance. (A) Determine the line's voltage and the minimum approach distance permitted under Table A (see § 1926.1408).” §1926.1411 Power line safety—while traveling under or near power lines with no load These procedures and criteria cover equipment traveling with no load under or near a power line on a construction site. Loaded travel falls under § 1926.1408, § 1926.1409 or § 1926.1410, whichever is appropriate, and § 1926.1417(u) [29cfr1926.1411(a)].

The employer must ensure the boom/mast and its support system are lowered sufficiently [29cfr1926.1411(b)(1)], Table T clearances are maintained [29cfr1926.1411(b)(2)], and speed and terrain effects, including boom/mast movement, are considered so they do not cause a breach of minimum clearance [29cfr1926.1411(b)(3)].

Table T minimums, by nominal AC voltage in kV, are: up to 0.75, 4 feet; over .75 to 50, 6 feet; over 50 to 345, 10 feet; over 345 to 750, 16 feet; over 750 to 1,000, 20 feet. Over 1,000, the distance is established by the utility owner/operator or a registered professional engineer qualified in electrical power transmission and distribution [29cfr1926.1411-table-T].

If any part of traveling equipment will get closer than 20 feet to the line, a dedicated spotter in continuous contact with you is required [29cfr1926.1411(b)(4)]. The spotter must be positioned to gauge clearance effectively, use direct communication equipment where necessary, and give you "timely information" so clearance can be maintained [29cfr1926.1411(b)(4)].

At night or in poor visibility, lines must also be illuminated or otherwise located, and a safe travel path identified and used [29cfr1926.1411(b)(5)]. “(i) The power lines are illuminated or another means of identifying the location of the lines is used. (ii) A safe path of travel is identified and used. §1926.1435(e)(5)(ii) Boom hoist limiting device “(ii) Boom hoist limiting device. The range of the boom must be limited at the minimum and maximum radius. Temporary alternative measures: Clearly mark the cable (so it can be seen by the operator) at a point that will give the operator sufficient time to stop the boom hoist within the minimum and maximum boom radius, or use a spotter who is in direct communication with the operator to inform the operator when this point is reached.” §1926.1401 Definitions These definitions control how the subpart's terms are read [29cfr1926.1401]. "Include/including" and "Such as" introduce non-exhaustive examples, and "Up to" means "up to and including." Load covers the hoisted objects and load-attaching equipment, such as the load block, ropes and slings, whether the term refers to the objects or their weight. Rated capacity is the manufacturer's maximum working load under specified conditions, typically involving configuration, radius and boom length [29cfr1926.1401].

Know your devices. A load moment (rated capacity) indicator compares the lifting condition with rated capacity and shows the percentage in use. A limiter, once rated capacity is reached, cuts power to functions that can increase loading severity; functions that reduce it typically remain operational. A boom hoist limiting device disengages boom hoist power at a predetermined angle and prevents lowering afterward by setting brakes or closing valves. Range control devices are operator-set: one limits boom or jib tip movement, the other warns. Operational aids provide information or automatically take control of a function, including those listed in § 1926.1416 [29cfr1926.1401].

For lowering, controlled load lowering uses the hoist drive motor rather than the load hoist brake. In free fall, only the brake regulates descent [29cfr1926.1401].

Near power lines, a dedicated spotter must meet § 1926.1428 and has the sole responsibility of watching separation and communicating with you so the minimum approach distance is not breached. A dedicated channel is assigned to "only one signal person and crane/derrick" or to a coordinated group. The employer controlling the communication system assigns it [29cfr1926.1401].

The fall zone extends beyond the area directly under the load to wherever suspended materials could foreseeably fall in an accident. Assembly/disassembly terms change for tower cranes to "erecting and climbing" and "dismantling." Any height increase is erection. Dismantling includes partial dismantling [29cfr1926.1401].

A multi-purpose machine is covered when configured with a winch pack, a jib with a hook, or a jib used with a winch, but not when configured with forks or tongs [29cfr1926.1401]. “With regard to tower cranes, “erecting and climbing” replaces the term “assembly,” and “dismantling” replaces the term “disassembly.” Regardless of whether the crane is initially erected to its full height or is climbed in stages, the process of increasing the height of the crane is an erection process. Assist crane means a crane used to assist in assembling or disassembling a crane. Attachments means any device that expands the range of tasks that can be done by the equipment. Examples include, but are not limited to: An auger, drill, magnet, pile-driver, and boom-attached personnel platform.”

The fall zone extends beyond the area directly under the load to wherever suspended materials could foreseeably fall in an accident. Assembly/disassembly terms change for tower cranes to "erecting and climbing" and "dismantling." Any height increase is erection. Dismantling includes partial dismantling [29cfr1926.1401].

A multi-purpose machine is covered when configured with a winch pack, a jib with a hook, or a jib used with a winch, but not when configured with forks or tongs [29cfr1926.1401].

With regard to tower cranes, “erecting and climbing” replaces the term “assembly,” and “dismantling” replaces the term “disassembly.” Regardless of whether the crane is initially erected to its full height or is climbed in stages, the process of increasing the height of the crane is an erection process. Assist crane means a crane used to assist in assembling or disassembling a crane. Attachments means any device that expands the range of tasks that can be done by the equipment. Examples include, but are not limited to: An auger, drill, magnet, pile-driver, and boom-attached personnel platform.

It covers at least the listed controls, drives, lines, hydraulic fluid, hooks, rope and reeving, electrical apparatus, tires, ground, level, windows, rail components and safety devices/aids. Disassembly or booming down is needed only if visual inspection or trial operation shows it. Determinations are reassessed during operation [29cfr1926.1412(d)(1)]. Level is checked against manufacturer tolerances before each shift and after each move and setup [29cfr1926.1412(d)(1)(xi)]. Ground and rail items have exceptions for certain FRA-regulated track [29cfr1926.1412(d)(1)(x)] [29cfr1926.1412(d)(1)(xiii)]. Hazardous deficiencies under items (i)-(xiii), or additional type-specific items, take equipment out of service until corrected [29cfr1926.1412(d)(2)]. Safety device/aid deficiencies require §§ 1926.1415 and 1926.1416 action before use [29cfr1926.1412(d)(3)].

Monthly, while in service, the shift inspection applies. Use waits until it shows no corrective action is required [29cfr1926.1412(e)(2)]. The inspecting employer documents it [29cfr1926.1412(e)(3)(i)] and retains it at least three months [29cfr1926.1412(e)(3)(ii)].

Qualified persons inspect safety- or capacity-affecting modifications [29cfr1926.1412(a)(1)], safety-related repairs/adjustments [29cfr1926.1412(b)(1)] and completed assemblies [29cfr1926.1412(c)(1)]. Hazards remove equipment from service until corrected, subject to specified temporary alternative measures [29cfr1926.1412(f)(5)]. Deficiencies needing monitoring must be checked monthly [29cfr1926.1412(f)(6)]. Records are retained at least 12 months [29cfr1926.1412(f)(7)].

Severe service requires stopping use and inspection [29cfr1926.1412(g)]. Equipment idle 3 months or more needs a qualified person's monthly inspection before use [29cfr1926.1412(h)]. Specified stricter manufacturer procedures apply [29cfr1926.1412(j)]. “(xii) Operator cab windows for significant cracks, breaks, or other deficiencies that would hamper the operator's view. The inspection must consist of observation for apparent deficiencies. Taking apart equipment components and booming down is not required as part of this inspection unless the results of the visual inspection or trial operation indicate that further investigation necessitating taking apart equipment components or booming down is needed.” §1926.1401 Definitions These definitions control how the subpart's terms are read [29cfr1926.1401]. "Include/including" and "Such as" introduce non-exhaustive examples, and "Up to" means "up to and including." Load covers the hoisted objects and load-attaching equipment, such as the load block, ropes and slings, whether the term refers to the objects or their weight. Rated capacity is the manufacturer's maximum working load under specified conditions, typically involving configuration, radius and boom length [29cfr1926.1401].

Know your devices. A load moment (rated capacity) indicator compares the lifting condition with rated capacity and shows the percentage in use. A limiter, once rated capacity is reached, cuts power to functions that can increase loading severity; functions that reduce it typically remain operational. A boom hoist limiting device disengages boom hoist power at a predetermined angle and prevents lowering afterward by setting brakes or closing valves. Range control devices are operator-set: one limits boom or jib tip movement, the other warns. Operational aids provide information or automatically take control of a function, including those listed in § 1926.1416 [29cfr1926.1401].

For lowering, controlled load lowering uses the hoist drive motor rather than the load hoist brake. In free fall, only the brake regulates descent [29cfr1926.1401].

Near power lines, a dedicated spotter must meet § 1926.1428 and has the sole responsibility of watching separation and communicating with you so the minimum approach distance is not breached. A dedicated channel is assigned to "only one signal person and crane/derrick" or to a coordinated group. The employer controlling the communication system assigns it [29cfr1926.1401].

The fall zone extends beyond the area directly under the load to wherever suspended materials could foreseeably fall in an accident. Assembly/disassembly terms change for tower cranes to "erecting and climbing" and "dismantling." Any height increase is erection. Dismantling includes partial dismantling [29cfr1926.1401].

A multi-purpose machine is covered when configured with a winch pack, a jib with a hook, or a jib used with a winch, but not when configured with forks or tongs [29cfr1926.1401]. “See Upperworks. Tagline means a rope (usually fiber) attached to a lifted load for purposes of controlling load spinning and pendular motions or used to stabilize a bucket or magnet during material handling operations. Tender means an individual responsible for monitoring and communicating with a diver. Tilt up or tilt down operation means raising/lowering a load from the horizontal to vertical or vertical to horizontal. Tower crane is a type of lifting structure which utilizes a vertical mast or tower to support a working boom (jib) in an elevated position.”

If the switch does not operate properly, the appointed person shall be immediately notified.” §1926.1401 Definitions These definitions control how the subpart's terms are read [29cfr1926.1401]. "Include/including" and "Such as" introduce non-exhaustive examples, and "Up to" means "up to and including." Load covers the hoisted objects and load-attaching equipment, such as the load block, ropes and slings, whether the term refers to the objects or their weight. Rated capacity is the manufacturer's maximum working load under specified conditions, typically involving configuration, radius and boom length [29cfr1926.1401].

Know your devices. A load moment (rated capacity) indicator compares the lifting condition with rated capacity and shows the percentage in use. A limiter, once rated capacity is reached, cuts power to functions that can increase loading severity; functions that reduce it typically remain operational. A boom hoist limiting device disengages boom hoist power at a predetermined angle and prevents lowering afterward by setting brakes or closing valves. Range control devices are operator-set: one limits boom or jib tip movement, the other warns. Operational aids provide information or automatically take control of a function, including those listed in § 1926.1416 [29cfr1926.1401].

For lowering, controlled load lowering uses the hoist drive motor rather than the load hoist brake. In free fall, only the brake regulates descent [29cfr1926.1401].

Near power lines, a dedicated spotter must meet § 1926.1428 and has the sole responsibility of watching separation and communicating with you so the minimum approach distance is not breached. A dedicated channel is assigned to "only one signal person and crane/derrick" or to a coordinated group. The employer controlling the communication system assigns it [29cfr1926.1401].

The fall zone extends beyond the area directly under the load to wherever suspended materials could foreseeably fall in an accident. Assembly/disassembly terms change for tower cranes to "erecting and climbing" and "dismantling." Any height increase is erection. Dismantling includes partial dismantling [29cfr1926.1401].

A multi-purpose machine is covered when configured with a winch pack, a jib with a hook, or a jib used with a winch, but not when configured with forks or tongs [29cfr1926.1401]. “Boom (tower cranes): On tower cranes, if the “boom” (i.e., principal horizontal structure) is fixed, it is referred to as a jib; if it is moveable up and down, it is referred to as a boom. Boom angle indicator means a device which measures the angle of the boom relative to horizontal. Boom hoist limiting device includes boom hoist disengaging device, boom hoist shut-off, boom hoist disconnect, boom hoist hydraulic relief, boom hoist kick-outs, automatic boom stop device, or derricking limiter.” §1926.1416(d)(1)(i)(B) “(B) Clearly mark the boom hoist cable (so that it can easily be seen by the operator) at a point that will give the operator sufficient time to stop the hoist to keep the boom within the minimum allowable radius. In addition, install mirrors or remote video cameras and displays if necessary for the operator to see the mark.”

§1926.1419(c)(1) “(1) When using hand signals, the Standard Method must be used (see appendix A of this subpart). Exception: Where use of the Standard Method for hand signals is infeasible, or where an operation or use of an attachment is not covered in the Standard Method, non-standard hand signals may be used in accordance with paragraph (c)(2) of this section.” §1926.1401 Definitions These definitions control how the subpart's terms are read [29cfr1926.1401]. "Include/including" and "Such as" introduce non-exhaustive examples, and "Up to" means "up to and including." Load covers the hoisted objects and load-attaching equipment, such as the load block, ropes and slings, whether the term refers to the objects or their weight. Rated capacity is the manufacturer's maximum working load under specified conditions, typically involving configuration, radius and boom length [29cfr1926.1401].

Know your devices. A load moment (rated capacity) indicator compares the lifting condition with rated capacity and shows the percentage in use. A limiter, once rated capacity is reached, cuts power to functions that can increase loading severity; functions that reduce it typically remain operational. A boom hoist limiting device disengages boom hoist power at a predetermined angle and prevents lowering afterward by setting brakes or closing valves. Range control devices are operator-set: one limits boom or jib tip movement, the other warns. Operational aids provide information or automatically take control of a function, including those listed in § 1926.1416 [29cfr1926.1401].

For lowering, controlled load lowering uses the hoist drive motor rather than the load hoist brake. In free fall, only the brake regulates descent [29cfr1926.1401].

Near power lines, a dedicated spotter must meet § 1926.1428 and has the sole responsibility of watching separation and communicating with you so the minimum approach distance is not breached. A dedicated channel is assigned to "only one signal person and crane/derrick" or to a coordinated group. The employer controlling the communication system assigns it [29cfr1926.1401].

The fall zone extends beyond the area directly under the load to wherever suspended materials could foreseeably fall in an accident. Assembly/disassembly terms change for tower cranes to "erecting and climbing" and "dismantling." Any height increase is erection. Dismantling includes partial dismantling [29cfr1926.1401].

A multi-purpose machine is covered when configured with a winch pack, a jib with a hook, or a jib used with a winch, but not when configured with forks or tongs [29cfr1926.1401]. “Stability (flotation device) means the tendency of a barge, pontoons, vessel or other means of flotation to return to an upright position after having been inclined by an external force. Standard Method means the protocol in appendix A of this subpart for hand signals. Such as means “such as, but not limited to.” Superstructure: See Upperworks. Tagline means a rope (usually fiber) attached to a lifted load for purposes of controlling load spinning and pendular motions or used to stabilize a bucket or magnet during material handling operations.” §1926.1419 Signals—general requirements Provide a signal person if the point of operation is not in your full view, the view in the travel direction is obstructed, or you or the load handler find one necessary for site-specific safety concerns [29cfr1926.1419(a)]. Signals must be hand, voice, audible or new [29cfr1926.1419(b)], and they and their means of transmission must suit site conditions [29cfr1926.1419(e)]. New signals require an employer demonstration [29cfr1926.1419(d)].

Use Standard Method hand signals unless that is infeasible or it does not cover the operation or attachment use [29cfr1926.1419(c)(1)]. Before using non-standard signals, the signal person, operator and any lift director must make contact and agree on them [29cfr1926.1419(c)(2)].

Safely stop operations requiring signals if transmission is interrupted. Wait until it is restored and a proper signal is given and understood [29cfr1926.1419(f)]. If you need to communicate a safety problem to the signal person, stop safely; resume only after you both agree it is resolved [29cfr1926.1419(g)].

Only one person signals at a time, subject to the paragraph (j) exception [29cfr1926.1419(h)]: anyone aware of a safety problem must alert you or the signal person with a stop or emergency stop signal [29cfr1926.1419(j)]. The section notes that § 1926.1417(y) requires you to obey it. Signal-person directions use your direction perspective [29cfr1926.1419(k)]. Across multiple cranes or derricks, identify the intended one before each function or direction, or use an equally effective method [29cfr1926.1419(m)]. “(3) Due to site specific safety concerns, either the operator or the person handling the load determines that it is necessary. §1926.1401 Definitions These definitions control how the subpart's terms are read [29cfr1926.1401]. "Include/including" and "Such as" introduce non-exhaustive examples, and "Up to" means "up to and including." Load covers the hoisted objects and load-attaching equipment, such as the load block, ropes and slings, whether the term refers to the objects or their weight. Rated capacity is the manufacturer's maximum working load under specified conditions, typically involving configuration, radius and boom length [29cfr1926.1401].

Know your devices. A load moment (rated capacity) indicator compares the lifting condition with rated capacity and shows the percentage in use. A limiter, once rated capacity is reached, cuts power to functions that can increase loading severity; functions that reduce it typically remain operational. A boom hoist limiting device disengages boom hoist power at a predetermined angle and prevents lowering afterward by setting brakes or closing valves. Range control devices are operator-set: one limits boom or jib tip movement, the other warns. Operational aids provide information or automatically take control of a function, including those listed in § 1926.1416 [29cfr1926.1401].

For lowering, controlled load lowering uses the hoist drive motor rather than the load hoist brake. In free fall, only the brake regulates descent [29cfr1926.1401].

Near power lines, a dedicated spotter must meet § 1926.1428 and has the sole responsibility of watching separation and communicating with you so the minimum approach distance is not breached. A dedicated channel is assigned to "only one signal person and crane/derrick" or to a coordinated group. The employer controlling the communication system assigns it [29cfr1926.1401].

The fall zone extends beyond the area directly under the load to wherever suspended materials could foreseeably fall in an accident. Assembly/disassembly terms change for tower cranes to "erecting and climbing" and "dismantling." Any height increase is erection. Dismantling includes partial dismantling [29cfr1926.1401].

A multi-purpose machine is covered when configured with a winch pack, a jib with a hook, or a jib used with a winch, but not when configured with forks or tongs [29cfr1926.1401]. “Articulating crane means a crane whose boom consists of a series of folding, pin connected structural members, typically manipulated to extend or retract by power from hydraulic cylinders. Assembly/Disassembly means the assembly and/or disassembly of equipment covered under this standard. With regard to tower cranes, “erecting and climbing” replaces the term “assembly,” and “dismantling” replaces the term “disassembly.” Regardless of whether the crane is initially erected to its full height or is climbed in stages, the process of increasing the height of the crane is an erection process.”

Walkways must be at least 12 inches wide. Guardrails and permanent attachments are not required. They are prohibited if removable, or on pendant-supported booms where ropes or bars could snag them. Otherwise, guardrails or railings may be no more than 45 inches high [29cfr1926.1423(b)(2)].

The employer must maintain originally equipped access hardware [29cfr1926.1423(c)(2)]. Post-date equipment needs safe access and egress, slip-resistant surfaces, and devices meeting specified SAE or ISO standards except where infeasible [29cfr1926.1423(c)(3)] [29cfr1926.1423(c)(4)].

Outside tower cranes, the employer must provide and ensure fall protection at unprotected sides or edges. In non-assembly/disassembly work, the trigger is more than 6 feet. When moving point-to-point, it covers non-lattice booms, non-horizontal lattice booms, and horizontal lattice booms with a fall distance of 15 feet or more. It also covers work stations anywhere on the equipment, except in the cab, on the deck, or at or near running draw-works [29cfr1926.1423(e)]. Assembly/disassembly uses more than 15 feet, with those same three exceptions [29cfr1926.1423(f)].

Tower cranes use more than 6 feet, with those exceptions, except for erecting, climbing and dismantling, where the trigger is more than 15 feet [29cfr1926.1423(h)].

Fall arrest and restraint systems use fall arrest components and either body belts or harnesses [29cfr1926.1423(d)]. Arrest and positioning systems go to any apparently substantial part unless a competent person would visually conclude, without engineering analysis, that the referenced criteria would not be met. Attachable anchors must meet those criteria. Restraint anchorages must withstand twice the maximum load an employee may impose in reasonably anticipated use [29cfr1926.1423(g)].

Hook or load-line anchoring for fall arrest requires a qualified person's capacity determination, an operator on site and informed, and no suspended load [29cfr1926.1423(j)].

(d) Load line free fall. In each of the following circumstances, controlled load lowering is required and free fall of the load line hoist is prohibited: (1) An employee is directly under the load. (4) The load is over a shaft.

§1926.1408(a)(2) “(2) Determine if any part of the equipment, load line or load (including rigging and lifting accessories), if operated up to the equipment's maximum working radius in the work zone, could get closer than 20 feet to a power line.” §1926.1427 Operator training, certification, and evaluation Covered equipment requires training, certification or licensing, and evaluation; otherwise, you operate only as a supervised trainee [29cfr1926.1427(a)(1)]. Derricks, sidebooms and equipment rated 2,000 pounds or less are excepted, but their training rules remain [29cfr1926.1427(a)(2)]. Military qualifications are employer-specific and last as the issuer stipulates [29cfr1926.1427(a)(3)].

Trainees need formal and practical instruction, assigned tasks within their ability, and continuous on-site monitoring by a qualified employer employee or agent doing nothing distracting [29cfr1926.1427(b)]. Non-tower cranes require line of sight plus verbal or hand signals; tower cranes require direct communication. Breaks are limited to 15 minutes, one per hour, after a task-and-limits briefing, with tasks within ability [29cfr1926.1427(b)(4)]. Uncertified trainees cannot work where equipment, line or load at maximum radius could reach within 20 feet of power lines up to 350 kV, or 50 feet above that voltage. They also cannot hoist personnel, make multiple-equipment lifts, or work over shafts or cofferdams or in tank farms. Multiple-lift rigging is barred unless the trainer finds their skills sufficient [29cfr1926.1427(b)(3)].

Qualifying state or local licensing governs within its jurisdiction (maximum validity 5 years); otherwise certification is required, with no employee cost [29cfr1926.1427(c)]. Accredited certification is type-based or type-and-capacity-based, portable among employers required to use that option, and valid 5 years; accreditation review occurs at least every 3 years [29cfr1926.1427(d)]. Audited-employer certification lasts 5 years and is not portable [29cfr1926.1427(e)(6)]. Audits occur within 3 months of program start, then at least every 3 years [29cfr1926.1427(e)(3)]. Significant deficiencies halt qualification until confirmed correction, require re-audit within 180 days afterward and an auditor's OSHA report within 15 days of determination; auditors keep audit records 3 years [29cfr1926.1427(e)(5)].

Evaluation covers safe operation, equipment-specific features and assigned hoisting [29cfr1926.1427(f)(1)]. Other equipment is allowed if the employer can demonstrate no substantially different abilities are needed [29cfr1926.1427(f)(5)]. Performance or knowledge evaluation indicating a need triggers retraining and subject re-evaluation [29cfr1926.1427(b)(5)] [29cfr1926.1427(f)(7)]. Pre-December 10, 2018 employees may be covered by prior assessments [29cfr1926.1427(f)(2)]. The section's effective date is December 10, 2018; evaluation and documentation, February 7, 2019 [29cfr1926.1427(k)]. “However, except as provided in paragraph (b)(3)(v) of this section, the operator-in-training shall not operate the equipment in any of the following circumstances unless certified in accordance with paragraph (c) of this section: (i) If any part of the equipment, load line, or load (including rigging and lifting accessories), if operated up to the equipment's maximum working radius in the work zone (see § 1926.1408(a)(1)), could get within 20 feet of a power line that is up to 350 kV, or within 50 feet of a power line that is over 350 kV.” §1926.1411 Power line safety—while traveling under or near power lines with no load These procedures and criteria cover equipment traveling with no load under or near a power line on a construction site. Loaded travel falls under § 1926.1408, § 1926.1409 or § 1926.1410, whichever is appropriate, and § 1926.1417(u) [29cfr1926.1411(a)].

The employer must ensure the boom/mast and its support system are lowered sufficiently [29cfr1926.1411(b)(1)], Table T clearances are maintained [29cfr1926.1411(b)(2)], and speed and terrain effects, including boom/mast movement, are considered so they do not cause a breach of minimum clearance [29cfr1926.1411(b)(3)].

Table T minimums, by nominal AC voltage in kV, are: up to 0.75, 4 feet; over .75 to 50, 6 feet; over 50 to 345, 10 feet; over 345 to 750, 16 feet; over 750 to 1,000, 20 feet. Over 1,000, the distance is established by the utility owner/operator or a registered professional engineer qualified in electrical power transmission and distribution [29cfr1926.1411-table-T].

If any part of traveling equipment will get closer than 20 feet to the line, a dedicated spotter in continuous contact with you is required [29cfr1926.1411(b)(4)]. The spotter must be positioned to gauge clearance effectively, use direct communication equipment where necessary, and give you "timely information" so clearance can be maintained [29cfr1926.1411(b)(4)].

At night or in poor visibility, lines must also be illuminated or otherwise located, and a safe travel path identified and used [29cfr1926.1411(b)(5)]. “(2) The clearances specified in Table T of this section are maintained. (3) The effects of speed and terrain on equipment movement (including movement of the boom/mast) are considered so that those effects do not cause the minimum clearance distances specified in Table T of this section to be breached. (4) Dedicated spotter. If any part of the equipment while traveling will get closer than 20 feet to the power line, the employer must ensure that a dedicated spotter who is in continuous contact with the driver/operator is used.”

§1926.1423(c)(4) “(4) Tower cranes manufactured after November 8, 2011 must be equipped so as to provide safe access and egress between the ground and the cab, machinery platforms, and tower (mast), by the provision of devices such as steps, handholds, ladders, and guardrails/railings/grabrails.” §1926.1401 Definitions These definitions control how the subpart's terms are read [29cfr1926.1401]. "Include/including" and "Such as" introduce non-exhaustive examples, and "Up to" means "up to and including." Load covers the hoisted objects and load-attaching equipment, such as the load block, ropes and slings, whether the term refers to the objects or their weight. Rated capacity is the manufacturer's maximum working load under specified conditions, typically involving configuration, radius and boom length [29cfr1926.1401].

Know your devices. A load moment (rated capacity) indicator compares the lifting condition with rated capacity and shows the percentage in use. A limiter, once rated capacity is reached, cuts power to functions that can increase loading severity; functions that reduce it typically remain operational. A boom hoist limiting device disengages boom hoist power at a predetermined angle and prevents lowering afterward by setting brakes or closing valves. Range control devices are operator-set: one limits boom or jib tip movement, the other warns. Operational aids provide information or automatically take control of a function, including those listed in § 1926.1416 [29cfr1926.1401].

For lowering, controlled load lowering uses the hoist drive motor rather than the load hoist brake. In free fall, only the brake regulates descent [29cfr1926.1401].

Near power lines, a dedicated spotter must meet § 1926.1428 and has the sole responsibility of watching separation and communicating with you so the minimum approach distance is not breached.
