§1926.1401 Definitions These definitions control how the subpart's terms are read [29cfr1926.1401]. "Include/including" and "Such as" introduce non-exhaustive examples, and "Up to" means "up to and including." Load covers the hoisted objects and load-attaching equipment, such as the load block, ropes and slings, whether the term refers to the objects or their weight. Rated capacity is the manufacturer's maximum working load under specified conditions, typically involving configuration, radius and boom length [29cfr1926.1401].

Know your devices. A load moment (rated capacity) indicator compares the lifting condition with rated capacity and shows the percentage in use. A limiter, once rated capacity is reached, cuts power to functions that can increase loading severity; functions that reduce it typically remain operational. A boom hoist limiting device disengages boom hoist power at a predetermined angle and prevents lowering afterward by setting brakes or closing valves. Range control devices are operator-set: one limits boom or jib tip movement, the other warns. Operational aids provide information or automatically take control of a function, including those listed in § 1926.1416 [29cfr1926.1401].

For lowering, controlled load lowering uses the hoist drive motor rather than the load hoist brake. In free fall, only the brake regulates descent [29cfr1926.1401].

Near power lines, a dedicated spotter must meet § 1926.1428 and has the sole responsibility of watching separation and communicating with you so the minimum approach distance is not breached. A dedicated channel is assigned to "only one signal person and crane/derrick" or to a coordinated group. The employer controlling the communication system assigns it [29cfr1926.1401].

The fall zone extends beyond the area directly under the load to wherever suspended materials could foreseeably fall in an accident. Assembly/disassembly terms change for tower cranes to "erecting and climbing" and "dismantling." Any height increase is erection. Dismantling includes partial dismantling [29cfr1926.1401].

A multi-purpose machine is covered when configured with a winch pack, a jib with a hook, or a jib used with a winch, but not when configured with forks or tongs [29cfr1926.1401]. “Instructions, diagrams, recommendations, warnings, specifications, protocols and limitations. Proximity alarm is a device that provides a warning of proximity to a power line and that has been listed, labeled, or accepted by a Nationally Recognized Testing Laboratory in accordance with 29 CFR 1910.7. Qualified evaluator (not a third party) means a person employed by the signal person's employer who has demonstrated that he/she is competent in accurately assessing whether individuals meet the Qualification Requirements in this subpart for a signal person.” §1926.1428 Signal person qualifications The signal person's employer must ensure each signal person meets the Qualification Requirements before giving any signals, using Option (1) or Option (2) [29cfr1926.1428(a)]. Option (1) relies on documentation from a third party qualified evaluator showing the person meets them [29cfr1926.1428(a)(1)]. Under Option (2), the employer's qualified evaluator assesses the person, determines that the requirements are met and documents that determination. This assessment "is not portable": other employers may not use it to meet this section [29cfr1926.1428(a)(2)].

Under either option, the documentation must be available at the site while the employer employs the signal person. It must specify each type of signaling, such as hand or radio signals, for which the person qualifies [29cfr1926.1428(a)(3)].

Qualification covers knowing the signals used, including the Standard Method if hand signals are used [29cfr1926.1428(c)(1)]; competence in applying them [29cfr1926.1428(c)(2)]; a basic understanding of equipment operation and limitations, including swing and stopping dynamics and boom deflection [29cfr1926.1428(c)(3)]; and the relevant requirements of §§ 1926.1419 through 1926.1422 and 1926.1428 [29cfr1926.1428(c)(4)]. These are demonstrated through an oral or written test and a practical test [29cfr1926.1428(c)(5)].

See § 1926.1417(f) and (j) for additional requirements.” §1926.1430 Training Your employer must train you on safe operation of the equipment you will use, in accordance with § 1926.1427(a) and (b) [29cfr1926.1430(c)(1)]. Operators covered under the exception in § 1926.1427(a)(2) must also be trained on safe operation of their equipment [29cfr1926.1430(c)(2)].

Operators of equipment covered by this subpart are trained in specific practices [29cfr1926.1430(c)(3)]. On friction equipment, whenever moving a boom off a support, you "first raise the boom a short distance", enough to take the boom's load, to determine whether the boom hoist brake needs adjustment. The practice also applies to other equipment with a boom. There, typically the brake can't be adjusted, so if it doesn't hold, "a repair is necessary". See also § 1926.1417(f) and (j) [29cfr1926.1430(c)(3)(i)]. Where available, training covers the manufacturer's emergency procedures for halting unintended equipment movement [29cfr1926.1430(c)(3)(ii)].

You also receive training in the tag-out and start-up procedures in § 1926.1417(f) and (g), as do other employees authorized to start or energize equipment or operate controls [29cfr1926.1430(f)]. Employees working with the equipment are trained on holes, crush/pinch points and § 1926.1424 hazards [29cfr1926.1430(e)].

Employers must evaluate required trainees to confirm understanding [29cfr1926.1430(g)(1)], give refresher training when conduct or a knowledge evaluation indicates retraining is necessary [29cfr1926.1430(g)(2)], and provide subpart CC training free to employees [29cfr1926.1430(g)(3)]. Other paragraphs address powerlines, signal persons, and competent and qualified persons [29cfr1926.1430(a)] [29cfr1926.1430(b)] [29cfr1926.1430(d)]. “(2) The employer must train each operator covered under the exception of § 1926.1427(a)(2) on the safe operation of the equipment the operator will be using. Appendix C to Subpart CC of Part 1926 (a)(4)(iii) “(iii) Insulated links.” §1926.1401 Definitions These definitions control how the subpart's terms are read [29cfr1926.1401]. "Include/including" and "Such as" introduce non-exhaustive examples, and "Up to" means "up to and including." Load covers the hoisted objects and load-attaching equipment, such as the load block, ropes and slings, whether the term refers to the objects or their weight. Rated capacity is the manufacturer's maximum working load under specified conditions, typically involving configuration, radius and boom length [29cfr1926.1401].

Know your devices. A load moment (rated capacity) indicator compares the lifting condition with rated capacity and shows the percentage in use. A limiter, once rated capacity is reached, cuts power to functions that can increase loading severity; functions that reduce it typically remain operational. A boom hoist limiting device disengages boom hoist power at a predetermined angle and prevents lowering afterward by setting brakes or closing valves. Range control devices are operator-set: one limits boom or jib tip movement, the other warns. Operational aids provide information or automatically take control of a function, including those listed in § 1926.1416 [29cfr1926.1401].

For lowering, controlled load lowering uses the hoist drive motor rather than the load hoist brake. In free fall, only the brake regulates descent [29cfr1926.1401].

Near power lines, a dedicated spotter must meet § 1926.1428 and has the sole responsibility of watching separation and communicating with you so the minimum approach distance is not breached. A dedicated channel is assigned to "only one signal person and crane/derrick" or to a coordinated group. The employer controlling the communication system assigns it [29cfr1926.1401].

The fall zone extends beyond the area directly under the load to wherever suspended materials could foreseeably fall in an accident. Assembly/disassembly terms change for tower cranes to "erecting and climbing" and "dismantling." Any height increase is erection. Dismantling includes partial dismantling [29cfr1926.1401].

Appendix B to Subpart CC of Part 1926 Appendix B to Subpart CC of Part 1926—Assembly/Disassembly: Sample Procedures for Minimizing the Risk of Unintended Dangerous Boom Movement For pin removal, the appendix cites § 1926.1404(f)(1): employees must not be under the boom, jib, or other components unless § 1926.1404(f)(2) is met. That exception applies when the employer demonstrates that site constraints require one or more employees to be there. The A/D director must then implement procedures that "minimize the risk of unintended dangerous movement and minimize the duration and extent of exposure under the boom" [29cfr1926.cc.appB].

In the sample, aboveground piping prevents lowering the boom, and the aerial lift, based on the near side, cannot be repositioned, so its basket must go under the boom. A rigged assist crane supports the detaching section, with particular care that the end near the pin removers is well supported. Far side pins come out first, the basket returns to the near side as soon as possible, then near side pins come out [29cfr1926.cc.appB].

During assembly/disassembly, the load's center of gravity must be identified if the stability method requires it. With insufficient information, measures must prevent unintended dangerous movement from misidentifying it. In the sample, the director cannot determine the pick point above a non-symmetrical top section's center of gravity. With personnel clear, it is raised a few inches to check for tipping. If it tips, the hoist line is repositioned and the test repeated until the director determines it can be moved without dangerous movement [29cfr1926.cc.appB]. “To minimize the risk of unintended dangerous movement while the pins are removed, the A/D director uses an assist crane that is rigged to support the boom section that is being detached, using particular care to ensure that the section end that is near the employee(s) removing the pins is well supported. The duration and extent of exposure is minimized by removing the far side pins first, moving the aerial lift basket as soon as possible to the near side so that the employees are no longer under the boom, and then removing the near side pins.”

Loads are permitted to be hoisted by such a winch while employees occupy the personnel platform only where the load on the winch line does not exceed 500 pounds and does not exceed the rated capacity of the winch and platform.” Appendix B to Subpart CC of Part 1926 Appendix B to Subpart CC of Part 1926—Assembly/Disassembly: Sample Procedures for Minimizing the Risk of Unintended Dangerous Boom Movement For pin removal, the appendix cites § 1926.1404(f)(1): employees must not be under the boom, jib, or other components unless § 1926.1404(f)(2) is met. That exception applies when the employer demonstrates that site constraints require one or more employees to be there. The A/D director must then implement procedures that "minimize the risk of unintended dangerous movement and minimize the duration and extent of exposure under the boom" [29cfr1926.cc.appB].

In the sample, aboveground piping prevents lowering the boom, and the aerial lift, based on the near side, cannot be repositioned, so its basket must go under the boom. A rigged assist crane supports the detaching section, with particular care that the end near the pin removers is well supported. Far side pins come out first, the basket returns to the near side as soon as possible, then near side pins come out [29cfr1926.cc.appB].

During assembly/disassembly, the load's center of gravity must be identified if the stability method requires it. With insufficient information, measures must prevent unintended dangerous movement from misidentifying it. In the sample, the director cannot determine the pick point above a non-symmetrical top section's center of gravity. With personnel clear, it is raised a few inches to check for tipping. If it tips, the hoist line is repositioned and the test repeated until the director determines it can be moved without dangerous movement [29cfr1926.cc.appB]. “A boom cannot be disassembled on the ground because of aboveground piping (as might be found, for example, in an oil refinery) that precludes lowering the boom to the ground. The boom must therefore be disassembled in the air, and the employees who remove the pins must perform that work from an aerial lift whose base is positioned on one side (the near side) of the boom. To gain access to the pins on the far side, the aerial lift basket must move under the boom, since, due to lack of room, the aerial lift cannot be repositioned on the far side.” §1910.184(c)(5) “(5) Slings used in a basket hitch shall have the loads balanced to prevent slippage.”

§1926.1432 Multiple-crane/derrick lifts—supplemental requirements These supplemental requirements apply to a crane/derrick operation in which more than one crane/derrick will be supporting the load. The operation must be planned before it begins [29cfr1926.1432(a)].

For the plan itself, a qualified person must develop it [29cfr1926.1432(a)(1)]. It must be designed "to ensure that the requirements of this subpart are met" [29cfr1926.1432(a)(2)]. A decision point concerns engineering: where the qualified person determines that engineering expertise is needed for the planning, the employer must ensure that it is provided [29cfr1926.1432(a)(3)].

For implementation, the lift must be directed by a lift director, and there are two acceptable arrangements [29cfr1926.1432(b)(1)]. The first is a single person who meets the criteria for both a competent person and a qualified person. The second is a competent person "who is assisted by one or more qualified persons" [29cfr1926.1432(b)(1)]. Under the wording of that paragraph, a competent person who does not also meet the qualified person criteria needs that assistance to fit either arrangement.

The lift director must also review the plan in a meeting with all workers who will be involved with the operation [29cfr1926.1432(b)(2)]. “The planning must meet the following requirements: (1) The plan must be developed by a qualified person. §1926.1401 Definitions These definitions control how the subpart's terms are read [29cfr1926.1401]. "Include/including" and "Such as" introduce non-exhaustive examples, and "Up to" means "up to and including." Load covers the hoisted objects and load-attaching equipment, such as the load block, ropes and slings, whether the term refers to the objects or their weight. Rated capacity is the manufacturer's maximum working load under specified conditions, typically involving configuration, radius and boom length [29cfr1926.1401].

Know your devices. A load moment (rated capacity) indicator compares the lifting condition with rated capacity and shows the percentage in use. A limiter, once rated capacity is reached, cuts power to functions that can increase loading severity; functions that reduce it typically remain operational. A boom hoist limiting device disengages boom hoist power at a predetermined angle and prevents lowering afterward by setting brakes or closing valves. Range control devices are operator-set: one limits boom or jib tip movement, the other warns. Operational aids provide information or automatically take control of a function, including those listed in § 1926.1416 [29cfr1926.1401].

For lowering, controlled load lowering uses the hoist drive motor rather than the load hoist brake. In free fall, only the brake regulates descent [29cfr1926.1401].

Near power lines, a dedicated spotter must meet § 1926.1428 and has the sole responsibility of watching separation and communicating with you so the minimum approach distance is not breached. A dedicated channel is assigned to "only one signal person and crane/derrick" or to a coordinated group. The employer controlling the communication system assigns it [29cfr1926.1401].

The fall zone extends beyond the area directly under the load to wherever suspended materials could foreseeably fall in an accident. Assembly/disassembly terms change for tower cranes to "erecting and climbing" and "dismantling." Any height increase is erection. Dismantling includes partial dismantling [29cfr1926.1401].

A multi-purpose machine is covered when configured with a winch pack, a jib with a hook, or a jib used with a winch, but not when configured with forks or tongs [29cfr1926.1401]. “Flange points are points of contact between rope and drum flange where the rope changes layers. Floating cranes/derricks means equipment designed by the manufacturer (or employer) for marine use by permanent attachment to a barge, pontoons, vessel or other means of flotation. For example means “one example, although there are others.” Free fall (of the load line) means that only the brake is used to regulate the descent of the load line (the drive mechanism is not used to drive the load down faster or retard its lowering).”

response.text: §1926.1435(e)(5)(iii) Anti two-blocking device “(iii) Anti two-blocking device. The tower crane must be equipped with a device which automatically prevents damage from contact between the load block, overhaul ball, or similar component, and the boom tip (or fixed upper block or similar component).” §1926.1431(d)(5)(v) Anti two-block “(v) Anti two-block. A device which automatically prevents damage and load failure from contact between the load block, overhaul ball, or similar component, and the boom tip (or fixed upper block or similar component) must be used. The device(s) must prevent such damage/failure at all points where two-blocking could occur. Exception: This device is not required when hoisting personnel in pile driving operations. Instead, paragraph (p)(2) of this section specifies how to prevent two-blocking during such operations.” §1926.1441(d)(2) Anti two-blocking “(2) Anti two-blocking. The employer must ensure that equipment covered by this section manufactured more than one year after November 8, 2010 have either an anti two-block device that meets the requirements of § 1926.1416(d)(3), or is designed so that, in the event of a two-block situation, no damage or load failure will occur (for example, by using a power unit that stalls in response to a two-block situation).”

response.text:
§1926.1435(e)(6)(v) Wind speed indicator “(v) Wind speed indicator. A device must be provided to display the wind speed and must be mounted above the upper rotating structure on tower cranes. On self erecting cranes, it must be mounted at or above the jib level. Temporary alternative measures: Use of wind speed information from a properly functioning indicating device on another tower crane on the same site, or a qualified person estimates the wind speed.” §1926.1401 Definitions These definitions control how the subpart's terms are read [29cfr1926.1401]. "Include/including" and "Such as" introduce non-exhaustive examples, and "Up to" means "up to and including." Load covers the hoisted objects and load-attaching equipment, such as the load block, ropes and slings, whether the term refers to the objects or their weight. Rated capacity is the manufacturer's maximum working load under specified conditions, typically involving configuration, radius and boom length [29cfr1926.1401].

Know your devices. A load moment (rated capacity) indicator compares the lifting condition with rated capacity and shows the percentage in use. A limiter, once rated capacity is reached, cuts power to functions that can increase loading severity; functions that reduce it typically remain operational. A boom hoist limiting device disengages boom hoist power at a predetermined angle and prevents lowering afterward by setting brakes or closing valves. Range control devices are operator-set: one limits boom or jib tip movement, the other warns. Operational aids provide information or automatically take control of a function, including those listed in § 1926.1416 [29cfr1926.1401].

For lowering, controlled load lowering uses the hoist drive motor rather than the load hoist brake. In free fall, only the brake regulates descent [29cfr1926.1401].

Near power lines, a dedicated spotter must meet § 1926.1428 and has the sole responsibility of watching separation and communicating with you so the minimum approach distance is not breached. A dedicated channel is assigned to "only one signal person and crane/derrick" or to a coordinated group. The employer controlling the communication system assigns it [29cfr1926.1401].

The fall zone extends beyond the area directly under the load to wherever suspended materials could foreseeably fall in an accident. Assembly/disassembly terms change for tower cranes to "erecting and climbing" and "dismantling." Any height increase is erection. Dismantling includes partial dismantling [29cfr1926.1401].

A multi-purpose machine is covered when configured with a winch pack, a jib with a hook, or a jib used with a winch, but not when configured with forks or tongs [29cfr1926.1401]. “It is typically used to support lattice boom sections during assembly/disassembly and under outrigger and stabilizer floats. Boatswain's chair means a single-point adjustable suspension scaffold consisting of a seat or sling (which may be incorporated into a full body harness) designed to support one employee in a sitting position. Bogie means “travel bogie,” which is defined below. Boom (equipment other than tower crane) means an inclined spar, strut, or other long structural member which supports the upper hoisting tackle on a crane or derrick.”

Near power lines, a dedicated spotter must meet § 1926.1428 and has the sole responsibility of watching separation and communicating with you so the minimum approach distance is not breached. A dedicated channel is assigned to "only one signal person and crane/derrick" or to a coordinated group. The employer controlling the communication system assigns it [29cfr1926.1401].

The fall zone extends beyond the area directly under the load to wherever suspended materials could foreseeably fall in an accident. Assembly/disassembly terms change for tower cranes to "erecting and climbing" and "dismantling." Any height increase is erection. Dismantling includes partial dismantling [29cfr1926.1401].

A multi-purpose machine is covered when configured with a winch pack, a jib with a hook, or a jib used with a winch, but not when configured with forks or tongs [29cfr1926.1401].

The center of gravity of any object is the point in the object around which its weight is evenly distributed. If you could put a support under that point, you could balance the object on the support. Certified welder means a welder who meets nationally recognized certification requirements applicable to the task being performed. Climbing means the process in which a tower crane is raised to a new working height, either by adding additional tower sections to the top of the crane (top climbing), or by a system in which the entire crane is raised inside the structure (inside climbing).

§1910.179(g)(1)(iii) “(iii) The voltage at pendant push-buttons shall not exceed 150 volts for a.c. and 300 volts for d.c.” §1926.1431(n) Hoisting personnel near power lines “(n) Hoisting personnel near power lines. Hoisting personnel within 20 feet of a power line that is up to 350 kV, and hoisting personnel within 50 feet of a power line that is over 350 kV, is prohibited, except for work covered by subpart V of this part (Power Transmission and Distribution).” §1926.1408 Power line safety (up to 350 kV)—equipment operations Before operating, the employer must identify the work zone: demarcated boundaries you are prohibited from passing, or 360 degrees out to maximum working radius [29cfr1926.1408(a)(1)]. If equipment, load line or load (with rigging and accessories) could get within 20 feet of a line at that radius, one option applies: utility-confirmed deenergizing with visible worksite grounding, 20-foot clearance, or Table A clearance [29cfr1926.1408(a)(2)]. Table A (AC, nominal kV): up to 50, 10 feet; over 50 to 200, 15; over 200 to 350, 20; over 350 to 500, 25; over 500 to 750, 35; over 750 to 1,000, 45; over 1,000, set by the utility or a qualified registered professional engineer. Upper values are inclusive [29cfr1926.1408-table-A]. Requested voltage information is due from the utility within two working days [29cfr1926.1408(c)].

Where encroachment precautions are required, there must be a planning meeting, non-conductive tag lines if used, and a flagged or high-visibility warning line, barricade or sign line in your view at the applicable distance [29cfr1926.1408(b)]. At least one measure is also required: proximity alarm, dedicated spotter, automatic warning device, automatic range limiter, or insulating link/device; subpart V work is excepted from this [29cfr1926.1408(b)(4)] [29cfr1926.1408(b)(5)]. If you cannot see the warning line, a dedicated spotter is required plus one of the other four [29cfr1926.1408(b)(3)]. Spotters need continuous contact, a visual aid, effective positioning, direct communication equipment where necessary, and must give timely information [29cfr1926.1408(b)(4)(ii)].

Operating below lines requires confirmed deenergizing and worksite grounding unless an exception applies [29cfr1926.1408(d)]. Presume lines energized [29cfr1926.1408(e)]. Near transmitter towers where charge could be induced, deenergize the transmitter, or ground the equipment and use only non-conductive tag lines if any [29cfr1926.1408(f)]. Training covers contact procedures, line presumptions, device limitations and grounding [29cfr1926.1408(g)(1)]. Safety devices, aids and contact-prevention means used for compliance must meet manufacturer procedures and conditions [29cfr1926.1408(h)]. “(iii) A device that automatically warns the operator when to stop movement, such as a range control warning device. Such a device must be set to give the operator sufficient warning to prevent encroachment. (iv) A device that automatically limits range of movement, set to prevent encroachment. (v) An insulating link/device, as defined in § 1926.1401, installed at a point between the end of the load line (or below) and the load. (5) The requirements of paragraph (b)(4) of this section do not apply to work covered by subpart V of this part. (c) Voltage information.”

§1926.1401 Definitions These definitions control how the subpart's terms are read [29cfr1926.1401]. "Include/including" and "Such as" introduce non-exhaustive examples, and "Up to" means "up to and including." Load covers the hoisted objects and load-attaching equipment, such as the load block, ropes and slings, whether the term refers to the objects or their weight. Rated capacity is the manufacturer's maximum working load under specified conditions, typically involving configuration, radius and boom length [29cfr1926.1401].

Know your devices. A load moment (rated capacity) indicator compares the lifting condition with rated capacity and shows the percentage in use. A limiter, once rated capacity is reached, cuts power to functions that can increase loading severity; functions that reduce it typically remain operational. A boom hoist limiting device disengages boom hoist power at a predetermined angle and prevents lowering afterward by setting brakes or closing valves. Range control devices are operator-set: one limits boom or jib tip movement, the other warns. Operational aids provide information or automatically take control of a function, including those listed in § 1926.1416 [29cfr1926.1401].

For lowering, controlled load lowering uses the hoist drive motor rather than the load hoist brake. In free fall, only the brake regulates descent [29cfr1926.1401].

§1926.1401 Definitions These definitions control how the subpart's terms are read [29cfr1926.1401]. "Include/including" and "Such as" introduce non-exhaustive examples, and "Up to" means "up to and including." Load covers the hoisted objects and load-attaching equipment, such as the load block, ropes and slings, whether the term refers to the objects or their weight. Rated capacity is the manufacturer's maximum working load under specified conditions, typically involving configuration, radius and boom length [29cfr1926.1401].

Know your devices. A load moment (rated capacity) indicator compares the lifting condition with rated capacity and shows the percentage in use. A limiter, once rated capacity is reached, cuts power to functions that can increase loading severity; functions that reduce it typically remain operational. A boom hoist limiting device disengages boom hoist power at a predetermined angle and prevents lowering afterward by setting brakes or closing valves. Range control devices are operator-set: one limits boom or jib tip movement, the other warns. Operational aids provide information or automatically take control of a function, including those listed in § 1926.1416 [29cfr1926.1401].

For lowering, controlled load lowering uses the hoist drive motor rather than the load hoist brake. In free fall, only the brake regulates descent [29cfr1926.1401].

Near power lines, a dedicated spotter must meet § 1926.1428 and has the sole responsibility of watching separation and communicating with you so the minimum approach distance is not breached. A dedicated channel is assigned to "only one signal person and crane/derrick" or to a coordinated group. The employer controlling the communication system assigns it [29cfr1926.1401].

The fall zone extends beyond the area directly under the load to wherever suspended materials could foreseeably fall in an accident. Assembly/disassembly terms change for tower cranes to "erecting and climbing" and "dismantling." Any height increase is erection. Dismantling includes partial dismantling [29cfr1926.1401].

A multi-purpose machine is covered when configured with a winch pack, a jib with a hook, or a jib used with a winch, but not when configured with forks or tongs [29cfr1926.1401]. “Marine worksite means a construction worksite located in, on or above the water. Mobile crane means a lifting device incorporating a cable suspended latticed boom or hydraulic telescopic boom designed to be moved between operating locations by transport over the road. Moving point-to-point means the times during which an employee is in the process of going to or from a work station. Multi-purpose machine means a machine that is designed to be configured in various ways, at least one of which allows it to hoist (by means of a winch or hook) and horizontally move a suspended load.”

§1910.184(f)(3) Safe operating temperatures “(3) Safe operating temperatures. Fiber core wire rope slings of all grades shall be permanently removed from service if they are exposed to temperatures in excess of 200 °F. When nonfiber core wire rope slings of any grade are used at temperatures above 400 °F or below minus 60 °F, recommendations of the sling manufacturer regarding use at that temperature shall be followed.” §1910.184(f)(5)(iv) “(iv) Evidence of heat damage.” §1910.184 Slings Inspect slings, fastenings and attachments daily before use, and during use as conditions warrant; a designated competent person does the daily check. Pull damaged or defective slings immediately [29cfr1910.184(d)]. Follow all safe practices on loading, rigging, identification and keeping clear; "Shock loading is prohibited." [29cfr1910.184(c)]. Five degrees or less from vertical may count as vertical [29cfr1910.184(b)].

Chain: thorough inspections at most 12 months apart [29cfr1910.184(e)(3)(i)]; proof test new, repaired or reconditioned slings before use [29cfr1910.184(e)(4)]. Remove permanently above 1000 degrees F; derate above 600 [29cfr1910.184(e)(6)]. Apply Table N-184-1 wear minimums (1⁄4-inch: 13⁄64) [29cfr1910.184(e)(8)] [29cfr1910.184-table-N-184-1]. Remove cracked or deformed components, and cracked hooks or hooks opened over 15 percent or twisted over 10 degrees [29cfr1910.184(e)(9)].

Wire rope: clear or circumferential minimums are 10, 40 or 96 diameters, by construction [29cfr1910.184(f)(2)]. Retire fiber-core slings exposed above 200 °F; for nonfiber core above 400 or below minus 60 °F, follow the manufacturer [29cfr1910.184(f)(3)]. Proof test welded attachments at twice capacity [29cfr1910.184(f)(4)(ii)]. Removal includes 10 random broken wires per lay or five in one strand per lay, one-third outer-wire diameter wear, and the 15-percent/10-degree hook limits, among other damage [29cfr1910.184(f)(5)].

Mesh: proof test at least 1 1/2 times capacity [29cfr1910.184(g)(5)]. Uncoated range is minus 20 to 550 °F; PVC or neoprene, zero to 200 °F [29cfr1910.184(g)(7)]. Removal limits include 25 per cent (abrasion), 15 (corrosion), 10 (slot depth or eye width) and 15 percent (handle-eye area) [29cfr1910.184(g)(9)].

Fiber rope: minus 20 to 180 °F, except wet frozen [29cfr1910.184(h)(2)]. Manila eye/short splices need three/six tucks; synthetic, four/eight. Rules also cover tails, 10-diameter clear length and 60-degree maximum eye angle [29cfr1910.184(h)(3)]. No repaired slings [29cfr1910.184(h)(6)].

Web: observe chemical restrictions [29cfr1910.184(i)(6)]; maximums are 180 °F (nylon, polyester) and 200 °F (polypropylene) [29cfr1910.184(i)(7)]. Proof test repairs to twice capacity [29cfr1910.184(i)(8)(ii)]. “(ii) Braided slings shall have a minimum clear length of wire rope 40 times the component rope diameter between the loops or end fittings. (iii) Cable laid grommets, strand laid grommets and endless slings shall have a minimum circumferential length of 96 times their body diameter. (3) Safe operating temperatures. Fiber core wire rope slings of all grades shall be permanently removed from service if they are exposed to temperatures in excess of 200 °F.”

Wire rope: clear or circumferential minimums are 10, 40 or 96 diameters, by construction [29cfr1910.184(f)(2)]. §1926.1432 Multiple-crane/derrick lifts—supplemental requirements These supplemental requirements apply to a crane/derrick operation in which more than one crane/derrick will be supporting the load. The operation must be planned before it begins [29cfr1926.1432(a)].

For the plan itself, a qualified person must develop it [29cfr1926.1432(a)(1)]. It must be designed "to ensure that the requirements of this subpart are met" [29cfr1926.1432(a)(2)]. A decision point concerns engineering: where the qualified person determines that engineering expertise is needed for the planning, the employer must ensure that it is provided [29cfr1926.1432(a)(3)].

For implementation, the lift must be directed by a lift director, and there are two acceptable arrangements [29cfr1926.1432(b)(1)]. The first is a single person who meets the criteria for both a competent person and a qualified person. The second is a competent person "who is assisted by one or more qualified persons" [29cfr1926.1432(b)(1)]. Under the wording of that paragraph, a competent person who does not also meet the qualified person criteria needs that assistance to fit either arrangement.

The lift director must also review the plan in a meeting with all workers who will be involved with the operation [29cfr1926.1432(b)(2)]. “§ 1926.1432 Multiple-crane/derrick lifts—supplemental requirements. The operation must be planned before it begins [29cfr1926.1432(a)].

For the plan itself, a qualified person must develop it [29cfr1926.1432(a)(1)]. It must be designed "to ensure that the requirements of this subpart are met" [29cfr1926.1432(a)(2)]. A decision point concerns engineering: where the qualified person determines that engineering expertise is needed for the planning, the employer must ensure that it is provided [29cfr1926.1432(a)(3)].

For implementation, the lift must be directed by a lift director, and there are two acceptable arrangements [29cfr1926.1432(b)(1)]. The first is a single person who meets the criteria for both a competent person and a qualified person. The second is a competent person "who is assisted by one or more qualified persons" [29cfr1926.1432(b)(1)]. Under the wording of that paragraph, a competent person who does not also meet the qualified person criteria needs that assistance to fit either arrangement.

The lift director must also review the plan in a meeting with all workers who will be involved with the operation [29cfr1926.1432(b)(2)]. “The planning must meet the following requirements: (1) The plan must be developed by a qualified person. §1926.1417(o)(3)(ii) “(ii) The operator must begin hoisting the load to determine, using a load weighing device, load moment indicator, rated capacity indicator, or rated capacity limiter, if it exceeds 75 percent of the maximum rated capacity at the longest radius that will be used during the lift operation. If it does, the operator must not proceed with the lift until he/she verifies the weight of the load in accordance with paragraph (o)(3)(i) of this section.” §1926.1403 Assembly/Disassembly—selection of manufacturer or employer procedures For assembly or disassembly of equipment or attachments, the employer has a fixed duty and a choice. The fixed duty is to comply with all applicable manufacturer prohibitions [29cfr1926.1403]. The choice is which procedures to comply with. The employer must use either the manufacturer procedures or its own [29cfr1926.1403].

The first option is the "Manufacturer procedures applicable to assembly and disassembly" [29cfr1926.1403(a)]. The second is employer procedures for assembly and disassembly [29cfr1926.1403(b)]. That second option is conditional: employer procedures may be used "only where the employer can demonstrate" that the procedures used meet the requirements in § 1926.1406 [29cfr1926.1403(b)]. In deciding between the two, keep in mind that the prohibitions duty is stated separately from the choice of procedures, so selecting employer procedures leaves applicable manufacturer prohibitions in force [29cfr1926.1403].

Synthetic slings affect this decision. According to the note, when an employer uses synthetic slings during assembly or disassembly rigging, the employer must follow manufacturer procedures [29cfr1926.1403-note-1]. The note refers to § 1926.1404(r) [29cfr1926.1403-note-1]. This section does not set out the contents of either § 1926.1406 or § 1926.1404(r). “When assembling or disassembling equipment (or attachments), the employer must comply with all applicable manufacturer prohibitions and must comply with either: (a) Manufacturer procedures applicable to assembly and disassembly, or (b) Employer procedures for assembly and disassembly. Employer procedures may be used only where the employer can demonstrate that the procedures used meet the requirements in § 1926.1406. Note: The employer must follow manufacturer procedures when an employer uses synthetic slings during assembly or disassembly rigging. (See § 1926.1404(r).)”

§1926.1402(e) “(e) If the A/D director or the operator determines that ground conditions do not meet the requirements in paragraph (b) of this section, that person's employer must have a discussion with the controlling entity regarding the ground preparations that are needed so that, with the use of suitable supporting materials/devices (if necessary), the requirements in paragraph (b) of this section can be met.” §1926.1402 Ground conditions Do not assemble or use the equipment unless the ground is firm, drained and graded enough to meet the manufacturer's specifications for adequate support and degree of level. You may count supporting materials, if necessary, toward meeting them. Drainage is not required in marshes or wetlands [29cfr1926.1402(b)]. Ground conditions include slope, compaction and firmness [29cfr1926.1402(a)(1)]. Supporting materials include blocking, mats, cribbing, marsh buggies in marshes or wetlands, and similar materials or devices [29cfr1926.1402(a)(2)].

The controlling entity must ensure the necessary ground preparations are provided [29cfr1926.1402(c)(1)]. It must also inform the equipment user and operator of the location of hazards beneath the set-up area, such as voids, tanks and utilities. The duty covers hazards identified in documents in its possession, on or off site, or hazards it otherwise knows about [29cfr1926.1402(c)(2)].

Without a controlling entity, the preparation duty in (c)(1) falls on the employer with authority at the site to make or arrange the preparations [29cfr1926.1402(d)].

If you, as operator, or the A/D director determine that conditions fall short, that person's employer must discuss the needed preparations with the controlling entity. The aim is to meet paragraph (b), using suitable supporting materials or devices if necessary [29cfr1926.1402(e)]. A limited exclusion applies to certain cranes on railroad tracks [29cfr1926.1402(f)]. “(c) The controlling entity must: (1) Ensure that ground preparations necessary to meet the requirements in paragraph (b) of this section are provided. (2) Inform the user of the equipment and the operator of the location of hazards beneath the equipment set-up area (such as voids, tanks, utilities) if those hazards are identified in documents (such as site drawings, as-built drawings, and soil analyses) that are in the possession of the controlling entity (whether at the site or off-site) or the hazards are otherwise known to that controlling entity.” §1926.1402(d) “(d) If there is no controlling entity for the project, the requirement in paragraph (c)(1) of this section must be met by the employer that has authority at the site to make or arrange for ground preparations needed to meet paragraph (b) of this section.”

body.text: §1910.180(d)(2) Regular inspection

The intervals in turn are dependent upon the nature of the critical components of the crane and the degree of their exposure to wear, deterioration, or malfunction. The two general classifications are herein designated as “frequent” and “periodic”, with respective intervals between inspections as defined below: (i) Frequent inspection: Daily to monthly intervals. (ii) Periodic inspection: 1- to 12-month intervals, or as specifically recommended by the manufacturer.

(i) A crane which has been idle for a period of one month or more, but less than 6 months, shall be given an inspection conforming with requirements of paragraph (d)(3) of this section and paragraph (g)(2)(ii) of this section before placing in service.
(xvii) Warning labels and decals originally supplied with the equipment by the manufacturer or otherwise required under this standard: Missing or unreadable.
